title: Telling Time Grade 2: Half Past & Quarter Past Made Easy + Free Quiz
meta_title: Telling Time Grade 2: Half Past & Quarter Past
meta_desc: Teach telling time grade 2 half past quarter on an analogue clock, plus a.m. vs p.m. and reading a calendar, with a free 8-question quiz and worksheet.
excerpt: In Grade 1 the clock only ever said o’clock. Grade 2 is where the minute hand starts to move — half past, quarter past, quarter to. Here is the order I teach it in, with a quick quiz to test your child.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a Grade 2 child a paper clock, set it to 6:30 and ask what time it is, and you will often hear ‘six… no, seven o’clock?’ The confusion is honest: the hour hand is sitting halfway between the 6 and the 7, so which one wins? Telling time grade 2 half past quarter is really the story of that in-between position — the moment a child stops reading only the o’clock and starts reading the minute hand too. In Grade 1 the clock only ever landed on a whole hour. Grade 2 is where it finally moves off it.

Below is the order I teach this in, built straight on top of the Grade-1 o’clock work. You need one thing the digital clock on the wall cannot give you: a proper analogue clock with two hands the child can turn by hand.

First, sort out the two hands

Before any child reads half past anything, they need to be certain which hand is which. Muddle the hands and every reading falls apart. I describe them by size, not colour, because colours vary from clock to clock.

  • The short, fat hand is the hour hand. It moves slowly and tells you roughly which hour you are in.
  • The long, thin hand is the minute hand. It moves faster and tells you how far into the hour you are.

A trick that sticks: the short word ‘hour’ goes with the short hand. Say it a few times and children stop guessing.

O’clock, then half past

Start on familiar ground. At o’clock the minute hand points straight up to the 12 and the hour hand points exactly at a number. Three o’clock: minute hand on 12, hour hand on 3. This is Grade 1 revision and it should take a minute.

Half past is the first new idea, and it is where that ‘six or seven?’ wobble lives. When the minute hand points straight down to the 6, half an hour has passed — the minute hand has swept halfway round the clock. The catch is that the hour hand has crept halfway too. At half past six the hour hand sits between the 6 and the 7. The rule I drill until it is automatic: for half past, name the hour the short hand has just left, not the one it is heading towards. Half past six, not half past seven.

Quarter past and quarter to

Once half past is solid, split each half in two. Think of the clock face as a pizza cut into four quarters.

Quarter past means the minute hand has travelled a quarter of the way round — it points to the 3, on the right-hand side. Fifteen minutes have gone. Quarter past four: minute hand on 3, hour hand a little past the 4.

Quarter to is the one children find hardest, because now we count what is left. The minute hand points to the 9, on the left-hand side, and there is a quarter of an hour still to go before the next o’clock. Quarter to five means fifteen minutes before five. Here the hour hand has moved almost all the way to the 5, which is exactly why quarter to trips them up — the short hand looks like it is already saying five, but we are naming the hour we are about to reach.

O’clock12 (straight up)0
Quarter past3 (right side)15
Half past6 (straight down)30
Quarter to9 (left side)45

a.m. and p.m. without the fuss

Grade 2 does not need the 24-hour clock, but children do need to know that 7 o’clock happens twice a day. Keep it concrete and tied to their own routine. In my experience the school day is the easiest anchor a seven-year-old has.

Simple version: a.m. is from midnight to noon — morning things, like breakfast and the school bell. p.m. is from noon to midnight — afternoon and evening things, like homework, dinner and bedtime. Ask ‘is 8 o’clock breakfast or bedtime?’ and let them decide which one it is. That is the whole idea at this level.

Days, months and reading a calendar

Time at Grade 2 is not only the clock. Children are also expected to read a calendar, and this half of the topic gets skipped far too often. There are seven days in a week and twelve months in a year, and both run in a fixed order — the same fixed-order idea that made the number line work.

Sit with an actual wall calendar and ask real questions. What day is the 15th? How many Sundays are in this month? If today is Wednesday, what day is it tomorrow? One honest caveat: do not rush to teach how many days each month has. ‘Thirty days has September’ can wait — recognising the order of the months and finding a date on the grid matters far more at seven.

A weekly routine that works

Ten minutes a day beats a long Sunday session. A pattern parents I know have used: two days turning the clock hands to o’clock and half past, two days on quarter past and quarter to, and one day on the calendar and a.m. versus p.m. The trick is to let the child set the clock, not just read it — making 3:30 with their own hands teaches far more than pointing at it.

Below is a short, free quiz covering exactly this — reading o’clock, half past, quarter past and quarter to, plus a.m., p.m. and the calendar. Let your child answer, then read the explanations together for anything they miss. quiz.title: Grade 2 Telling Time Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on reading an analogue clock — o’clock, half past, quarter past and quarter to — plus a.m., p.m. and the calendar. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 2 telling time to the half and quarter hour

questions.q: Which hand tells you the hour?
questions.explanation: The short, fat hand is the hour hand. The short word ‘hour’ goes with the short hand.

questions.q: The minute hand points straight down to the 6. What time of the hour is it?
questions.explanation: When the minute hand points to the 6, half an hour has passed, so it is half past.

questions.q: The hour hand is between the 4 and the 5, and the minute hand is on the 6. What time is it?
questions.explanation: For half past, name the hour the short hand has just left. It left the 4, so it is half past 4.

questions.q: Where does the minute hand point at quarter past?
questions.explanation: Quarter past means the minute hand has gone a quarter of the way round to the 3 on the right.

questions.q: The minute hand points to the 9. Which time is this?
questions.explanation: The minute hand on the 9 means a quarter of an hour is left before the next hour, so it is quarter to.

questions.q: How many minutes are there in a quarter of an hour?
questions.explanation: A quarter of an hour is 15 minutes. Half an hour is 30 minutes.

questions.q: Which of these usually happens in the a.m.?
questions.explanation: a.m. runs from midnight to noon, so breakfast is a morning, a.m. activity.

questions.q: How many days are there in one week?
questions.explanation: There are 7 days in a week. There are 12 months in a year.

faq.q: What time skills should a child have by the end of Grade 2?
faq.a: Reading an analogue clock to o’clock, half past, quarter past and quarter to, knowing which hand is which, telling a.m. from p.m. in simple terms, and finding a date on a calendar. Some children reach this sooner and some a term later — both are fine.

faq.q: Why does my child say half past seven when the clock shows half past six?
faq.a: Because at half past the hour hand has already crept past the 6 towards the 7, so it looks like seven. The rule that fixes it: for half past, name the hour the short hand has just left, not the one it is heading to.

faq.q: Should I teach the digital clock or the analogue clock first?
faq.a: Analogue first, by a wide margin. The moving hands show how far through the hour you are, which is the whole point of half past and quarter past. Digital time makes more sense once a child can already read a clock face.

faq.q: Is my child too young for a.m. and p.m. in Grade 2?
faq.a: No, as long as you keep it concrete. Skip the 24-hour clock and just link a.m. to morning routines and p.m. to afternoon and evening ones. Ask ‘breakfast or bedtime?’ and let them reason it out.
